title: Indians Bear the Brunt as Canada's Student Visa Crackdown Sends Permit Approvals Plummeting
excerpt: India's share of new Canadian study permits collapsed from 51.6% in 2023 to 8.1% by late 2025, with rejection rates hitting 74% as Ottawa tightens immigration controls.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India's share of Canadian study permits plummeted from 51.6% in 2023 to 8.1% by 2025.
  • Rejection rates for Indian student visa applicants soared to 74% in August 2025, up from 32% two years prior.
  • Indian study permit applications dropped from 19,175 in August 2023 to 3,920 by August 2025.
  • Canada froze new applications under its Parents and Grandparents Program, impacting family reunification for Indians.
  • Total Indian students abroad decreased from 8.92 lakh in 2023 to 7.59 lakh in 2024, with Canada seeing a 41% drop.

  • India's share of new Canadian study permits collapsed from 51.6% in 2023 to just 8.1% by September 2025, the steepest decline in more than a decade.
  • Rejection rates for Indian student visa applicants hit 74% in August 2025, compared to 32% two years earlier and 40% for applicants globally.
  • The number of Indian applicants dropped from 19,175 in August 2023 to 3,920 in August 2025, as Ottawa cited fraud concerns and capped permits for the second consecutive year.
  • Canada has also frozen new applications under its Parents and Grandparents Program, cutting another reunification pathway for Indian families.

Canada's multi-year crackdown on international student admissions has hit Indian applicants harder than any other nationality, with data showing a near-total collapse in the pipeline that once made Canada the top destination for Indian students seeking degrees abroad.

According to Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) data reported by Reuters, about 74% of Indian applications for study permits at Canadian post-secondary institutions were rejected in August 2025 — more than double the 32% rejection rate just two years earlier. By contrast, the overall refusal rate for all nationalities stood at roughly 40%, and Chinese applicants faced a 24% rejection rate.

The Numbers Tell a Stark Story

The volume of Indian applicants has plunged alongside the rising rejection rates. In August 2023, 19,175 Indians applied for study permits; by August 2025, that number had fallen to 3,920. India's share of all new Canadian study permits fell from 51.6% in 2023 to 8.1% by September 2025, according to IRCC data cited in a parliamentary committee report.

> **"Jaspreet Singh, founder of the International Sikh Students Association, recalled government posters that once exhorted newcomers to "Study, work, stay" in Canada."**

"Jaspreet Singh, founder of the International Sikh Students Association, recalled government posters that once exhorted newcomers to "Study, work, stay" in Canada."

Active study permits held by Indian students in Canada declined from 319,000 in 2023 to 226,000 in 2024, the steepest year-on-year fall in more than a decade. The ApplyBoard recruitment firm described the shift as "seismic," noting that just 4,210 new permits were issued to Indian students in March 2025 — an 85% drop from 28,073 in the same month the previous year.

Why Canada Tightened the Rules

Ottawa has framed the crackdown as a response to fraud and housing pressure. In 2023, Canadian authorities uncovered nearly 1,550 study permit applications linked to fraudulent letters of acceptance, most originating from India, the immigration department told Reuters. Its beefed-up verification system detected more than 14,000 potentially fraudulent letters the following year.

The Canadian government lowered the cap on international student permits for the second consecutive year in early 2025, setting a national limit of 408,000 permits for 2026. A parliamentary committee has recommended an India-specific country cap, citing data showing India ranked first for asylum claims made while holding student permits in both 2024 and 2025.

"Some of the best quality students available in the world are from India, and Canadian institutions have in the past greatly benefited from the talent and academic excellence of these students."

— Indian Embassy in Ottawa

The Impact on Universities and Families

The University of Waterloo, home to Canada's largest engineering school, has seen a two-thirds decline in Indian students entering its undergraduate and graduate programs over four years. The University of Regina and the University of Saskatchewan have reported similar drops. Conestoga College, once among the largest recipients of Indian students, cut 80 programs and reduced its workforce by about 1,800 faculty and staff.

The blow extends beyond campuses. Canada froze new applications under its Parents and Grandparents Program (PGP) on July 15, 2026, citing a backlog of nearly 60,000 applications. The program has been a critical family reunification pathway for the Indian diaspora, particularly from Punjab's Doaba and Malwa regions.

Ministry of External Affairs data shows total Indian students going abroad fell from 8.92 lakh in 2023 to 7.59 lakh in 2024. Canada saw the steepest decline — a 41% drop from 233,532 to 137,608. The US and UK also registered declines, while non-traditional destinations such as Bangladesh, Uzbekistan, Russia, and Singapore gained ground.

For the diaspora community, the reversal is jarring. Jaspreet Singh, founder of the International Sikh Students Association, recalled government posters that once exhorted newcomers to "Study, work, stay" in Canada. "That attitude has soured," he told Reuters. Some recently rejected applicants, he added, are taking it in stride: "They are happy they didn't come."
